title: Maryland Crab Cakes
subtitle: Pan-fried crab cakes with Old Bay seasoning
excerpt: Maryland crab cakes are mostly crab, bound with just enough breadcrumb and egg to hold together, not padded out like lesser versions. The binding is minimal so the crab flavour dominates. They're seasoned with Old Bay, which is the compulsory spice blend for anything from the Chesapeake.
sourceNotes: Maryland crab cakes are the defining dish of Chesapeake Bay cuisine. The minimal-binding, mostly-crab formula is the Baltimore and Maryland standard that distinguishes them from heavily padded versions found elsewhere.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze before cooking, on a tray, then bag. Thaw overnight in the fridge before frying.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Shape and refrigerate for up to 24 hours before frying.

content.text: Maryland crab cakes are bound with just enough to hold together, not enough to dilute. The standard formula is crab meat, a little mayonnaise, an egg, a spoonful of mustard, and enough breadcrumbs to prevent total collapse, nothing more. Old Bay seasoning is not negotiable: it's the flavour that makes a Maryland crab cake distinct from any other.

Old Bay is an American spice blend created in Baltimore in 1939, containing celery salt, paprika, black pepper, and a mixture of spices. It's sold in UK supermarkets and online. If you can't find it, make a rough substitute: 1 tsp celery salt, 1 tsp paprika, ¼ tsp each of black pepper, cayenne, and dried thyme.

items.prepNote: white and brown mixed, drained of any liquid

content.text: Combine {{mayonnaise}}, {{eggs}}, {{dijon-mustard}}, {{worcestershire-sauce}}, {{old-bay-seasoning}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}} in a large bowl. Add {{crab-meat}}, {{panko}}, {{flat-leaf-parsley}}, and {{spring-onion}}. Mix gently. Keep the crab in pieces, not mashed.
Divide into eight equal portions. Shape each into a cake about 2 cm thick. Arrange on a tray lined with baking paper and refrigerate for one hour to firm up.

Heat {{rapeseed-oil}} and {{unsalted-butter}} in a wide frying pan over medium-high heat. When the butter stops foaming, add the crab cakes in batches. Cook for three to four minutes without moving until a golden crust forms, then flip carefully and cook for three to four minutes more. Serve with a wedge of lemon and tartar sauce or soured cream.

items.symptom: The crab cakes fall apart when turned
items.cause: Not enough chilling time, or too much moisture in the crab meat.
items.fix: Drain the crab thoroughly. An hour's chilling is the minimum; longer is better. Use a wide spatula and flip in one confident move. If they're still fragile, add another tablespoon of panko to the remaining mix.

items.symptom: The cakes are more breadcrumb than crab
items.fix: 50 g of panko for 450 g of crab is the ratio: the mixture should look mostly crab with just enough binding to hold it together. Reduce the panko to 30 g for the most crab-forward version.

items.cause: Pan not hot enough when the cakes go in, or too much oil.
items.fix: The pan should be hot enough that the butter is foaming vigorously when you add the cakes. The oil-butter combination is enough; don't add more.

items.symptom: The seasoning is flat even with Old Bay
items.cause: Not enough salt, or Old Bay quantity too low.
items.fix: Old Bay contains salt (celery salt) but the crab mixture still needs additional seasoning. Taste the mixture before shaping: it should be noticeably well seasoned.

content.text: Maryland crab cakes are the centrepiece of Chesapeake Bay cuisine. The blue crab of the Chesapeake, smaller and sweeter than Atlantic or Pacific crab, is the traditional ingredient, and the regional pride attached to crab cakes is fierce. Marylanders insist that real crab cakes should taste of crab, not filler. Serve simply: lemon, a little sauce, and nothing that competes with the main ingredient.
